title: Dialogue Writing — natural conversation between speakers
notes: **What it is:** a purposeful conversation on the page — natural turns, not monologues.

**Structure:** Optional context line → Speaker names + colon per turn → short natural exchanges (1–2 sentences) pushing toward the aim (question → answer → problem → solution) → a resolving close ('Deal.').

**Naturalness grammar:** contractions everywhere; fillers and tags ('You know what', 'Honestly speaking', '…right?'); short reactions ('Exactly!', 'No way!'); tense follows context (will/would for plans, past for stories).
**Voice test:** give each character a distinguishable style — one formal, one playful — and read the exchange aloud.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Complete dialogue template:**
[Context line — optional but helpful: 'In the school corridor, two friends are discussing the upcoming sports day.']

[Amit]: Hey, did you hear about the relay race?
[Binita]: Yeah! I just signed up. What about you?
[Amit]: I'm thinking of joining too, but I'm scared I'll drop the baton.
[Binita]: Don't worry, we'll practice together. Remember last year's race?
[Amit]: Yeah, we finished third. This time, let's aim for first.
[Binita]: Deal. First thing tomorrow — practice session at the field.

**Dialogue structure — the conversational arc:** Every dialogue has a purpose. It's not just two people chatting. Structure: (1) *Opening* — establish who's talking and the situation ('Hey, did you hear…'); (2) *Exchange* — questions and answers, reactions and counters ('Yeah! I just signed up.' / 'What about you?'); (3) *Conflict/Tension* — the problem or disagreement ('I'm scared I'll drop the baton.'); (4) *Resolution* — solution or agreement ('Don't worry, we'll practice together.') Every dialogue should move from A to B — from unknown to known, from problem to solution, from doubt to decision.

**Making dialogue sound natural — the 4 rules:** (1) *Contractions*: 'I'm', 'don't', 'can't', 'you're', 'we'll' — never 'I am', 'do not', 'cannot'. (2) *Short sentences*: Real speech is fragmentary. 'No way!' 'Seriously?' 'I don't know.' (3) *Overlapping/interjections*: 'Wait, actually…' 'But—' 'Oh, right!' (4) *Repetition for emphasis*: 'I really, REALLY don't want to go.' Natural dialogue is messy. Perfect grammar kills the realism.

**Voice differentiation — giving characters personality:** Each character should have a distinguishable voice. Compare: Character A (formal): 'I believe that option A presents the most viable solution.' Character B (informal): 'Nah, option B's way better, trust me.' Now contrast: Both formal: they sound the same. Both informal: indistinguishable. The key is CONTRAST — different vocabularies, different sentence lengths, different attitudes. Even siblings should sound different when you remove the name tags.

**Dialogue tags and action beats — keeping it alive:** Don't overuse 'said' and 'asked' — they're invisible and fine. But mix in action beats: [She looked out the window, her voice barely above a whisper.] [He slammed the door, his face red with anger.] Action beats are MORE powerful than tags because they show emotion instead of telling it. Use tags like 'whispered', 'muttered', 'exclaimed', 'snapped' only when 'said' doesn't convey the emotion.

**What dialogue should NOT contain:** (1) *Excessive exposition* — 'As you know, Bob, since our parents died in the accident five years ago, we've lived with our aunt…' (real people don't explain obvious things to each other); (2) *Perfect grammar* — people interrupt, trail off, repeat themselves; (3) *Monologues* — one person talking for 5 lines; (4) *Unnecessary pleasantries* — 'Hello, how are you?' 'I'm fine, thank you.' (Cut to the point); (5) *Both characters agreeing all the time* — conflict creates drama. Even small disagreements ('I think we should…' 'No, we should…') make dialogue dynamic.

**Context line — the invisible setup:** A context line (italic or plain) sets the scene before dialogue starts: 'At the bus stop, two strangers begin talking.' This helps the examiner understand the situation without your dialogue having to explain it. Keep context lines SHORT and relevant. Don't over-describe — the dialogue should show the scene, not the context line.

**Speaker identification — format conventions:** In exams, the standard format is: [Name]: [dialogue]. Alternative formats accepted: [Name says], [dialogue] OR [Name]: [dialogue]. Key rules: (1) Name followed by colon; (2) One line of dialogue per speaker (usually); (3) Name changes on every new speaker line; (4) Consistent formatting throughout — don't switch from 'Rahul:' to 'Rahul said:' mid-dialogue.

**Dialogue for different purposes — exam scenarios:** (1) *Persuasion*: One character tries to convince the other. (2) *Conflict resolution*: Two characters disagree and find common ground. (3) *Information exchange*: One character learns something from the other. (4) *Emotional support*: One character comforts the other. (5) *Decision making*: Two characters decide on a course of action. (6) *Humour*: Light, playful exchange. Know which purpose your dialogue serves — it shapes every line.

**Common dialogue writing errors:** (1) Both characters sound the same — no voice differentiation. (2) Too formal — 'I do not understand what you mean.' (3) No purpose — two people chatting about nothing. (4) Wrong format — no speaker names, or inconsistent formatting. (5) Monologues — one character talks for 6 lines. (6) Over-use of 'said' with adverbs — 'he said angrily', 'she said sadly'. (7) Unrealistic exposition — characters explaining things they already know. (8) No conflict or tension — everyone agrees all the time. (9) Forgetting the context. (10) Exceeding the word limit with one long exchange.

**The read-aloud test for dialogue:** Read your dialogue aloud with two different voices — one for each character. If you can't distinguish them by voice alone (without reading the names), the dialogue needs more differentiation. Also: does it sound like REAL people talking? If it sounds like an essay with 'said' inserted, rewrite it. Dialogue should sound like life, not like literature.
confusion: Dialogue vs. Conversation: All dialogues are conversations, but not all conversations are dialogues. A 'dialogue' in exam writing has a PURPOSE — it must advance a plot, reveal character, or resolve a conflict. A casual conversation ('Nice weather today') without purpose is not a dialogue. Every line should move the interaction forward.

Dialogue tags vs. action beats: 'Said' and 'asked' are tags that identify WHO is speaking. Action beats ('She looked away, fiddling with her hair') show WHAT the character is doing while speaking. Tags are necessary for clarity; action beats are necessary for drama. Use tags for unknown speakers, action beats for emotional moments. Never overuse both.

First person dialogue vs. narrative: Dialogue is what characters SAY. Narrative is what the NARRATOR tells. 'I walked into the room' is narrative. 'Walked into the room?' she asked. is dialogue. Never confuse them. In a dialogue task, you're writing spoken words between characters, not describing what happens to them.

Quotation marks in dialogue vs. prose: In English dialogue, each speaker's line is enclosed in quotation marks when written as prose ('I don't agree,' he said. 'This plan will fail.'). In exam dialogue format (Name: dialogue), quotation marks are usually NOT used because the name label already identifies the speaker. Check your exam's preferred format.

Formal dialogue vs. informal dialogue: The register of your dialogue should match the characters' relationship. Two students talking casually can use slang, contractions, and fragmented sentences. Two officials discussing policy should use formal language, complete sentences, and precise vocabulary. Mixing registers (a teacher speaking like a teenager, or a friend speaking like a lawyer) sounds unnatural and loses marks.
practice: Write a dialogue (120-150 words) between two friends discussing their plans for the coming holidays. Give each character a distinct voice — one optimistic and planning-oriented, the other practical and cautious. Include at least one action beat.

Write a dialogue (100-120 words) between a student and a teacher. The student is asking for an extension on an assignment because of illness. The teacher is sympathetic but firm about deadlines. Show the teacher's care through dialogue, not description.

Write a dialogue (120 words) between two siblings. One wants to go to college in Kathmandu; the other wants to stay in Pokhara. Show their disagreement through natural back-and-forth, not exposition. End with a compromise or an unresolved tension.

Read this dialogue and identify THREE weaknesses: 'Rahul: Hello Priya. How are you?' Priya: I am fine, thank you. And you?' Rahul: I am also fine. Priya: What would you like to discuss?' Rahul: I would like to discuss the project.' Rewrite it to make it natural and purposeful.

Write a dialogue (100-120 words) between a parent and a child. The child has just received bad exam results. The parent is disappointed but supportive. Use action beats to show emotion. Keep the dialogue realistic — parents don't deliver monologues.
universalFacts: The dialogue as a literary device dates back to ancient Greek philosophy, where Plato wrote his teachings in the form of conversations between Socrates and his students. The Socratic dialogue — questioning, probing, leading to insight — remains the gold standard for purposeful dialogue in literature and drama.

In the NEB English exam, dialogue writing carries 5-8 marks. Common issues: (1) both characters sound identical, (2) no conflict or tension, (3) unnatural exposition, (4) wrong format. The most important skill tested is 'voice differentiation' — can you make two characters sound like different people?

Scriptwriters use a technique called 'subtext' — what characters mean but don't say. In exams, you can't write subtext directly (you only write what is said), but you can imply it through dialogue. 'I'm fine' said with an action beat like 'she looked out the window' implies she is NOT fine. This subtle technique earns higher marks.

The most famous dialogue writers in English literature include William Shakespeare (his characters are instantly distinguishable by speech patterns), Jane Austen (her dialogue reveals social class and personality), and Ernest Hemingway (his dialogue is sparse, natural, and loaded with subtext). Studying these writers improves your dialogue writing significantly.

A study of bestselling novels found that dialogue comprising 20-40% of the text tends to be most engaging. Less than 20% feels like a narrative report; more than 40% can feel like a script. The 'sweet spot' for dialogue depends on genre — fiction allows more, but every line must earn its place.
